Representative_Docs: [' The Ontario government is making a major move in support of journalism in the province. Premier Doug Ford has instructed his ministers that as of September, a significant portion of the province\'s advertising budget must be spent with Ontario media outlets. Perhaps more importantly, Ford has instructed his ministers in charge of the province\'s four biggest agencies, in terms of advertising, to do the same. Letters have now been sent to the chairs of the Ontario Lottery and Gaming Commission, the Liquor Control Board of Ontario, Metrolinx and the Ontario Cannabis Store. Starting later this summer, each of these agencies will be required to set aside 25 per cent of their advertising budget for provincially based sources."Ontario\'s major government agencies are some of the largest advertisers in the province, together spending well over $100 million on marketing each year," the letters state. "These significant advertising budgets should help support Ontario-based publishers and the Ontario-based workers creating local news content for people in our province."In the letters to the organizations, the Ford government states that they want the Crown agencies to spend more advertising with "Ontario-based corporations, trusts or partnerships that have been designated as Qualified Canadian Journalism Organizations by the Canada Revenue Agency."The list of organizations qualified by the federal government includes small and large publications including titles owned by Postmedia, owner of the Toronto Sun as well as other such newspapers as the National Post, London Free Press and Ottawa Citizen. Community publications such as The Creemore Echo or specialized publications such as The Trillium newsletter covering Queen\'s Park also qualify. Governments of all stripes and at all levels across the country have said that they want to support journalism, but few have been willing to do so, putting most of their money into Google and Facebook products. The latest annual report from the federal government shows that they spent $1.1 million advertising on TikTok in fiscal year 2022-23 despite all the security concerns around the social media app which has been banned from government devices. By comparison, the Trudeau government spent just $944,602 on print advertising across Canada in the same year. TikTok received more advertising from the federal government that fiscal year than every Postmedia newspaper, the Toronto Star, the Globe and Mail, Journal de Montreal and every community newspaper combined. It\'s an odd message for the federal government to send to the media industry, saying that we are vital for news organizations\'future but we\'re just going to spend all of our advertising with digital giants. The federal government, which currently spends 71 per cent of their advertising budget on digital, should consider a similar move to what Ford is pushing through. It would be a far better way to support journalism and homegrown media outlets than giving all your money to Facebook and Google while sending subsidy cheques to media companies. In the latest federal advertising report, $9.9 million is spent on search engine marketing, the same amount it spent on all television advertising across Canada. The bulk of that money goes to Google, while most of the $13 million the feds spend on social media marketing goes to Meta, the parent company of Facebook and Instagram. In the most recent Review of Government Advertising by the auditor general for Ontario, $4.5 million out of $28.8 million of Ontario government ad spending went to print advertising. That works out to roughly 16 per cent of all reviewable Ontario government ads. While the directive letters are aimed at the four main agencies and their advertising budgets, the Ford government will go further and require the same 25 per cent of all government advertising spending be placed with Ontario publishers."When in place across Ontario\'s major agencies, this new initiative promises to flow over $25 million to Ontario-based publishers, helping to protect jobs and promote local content and culture," Finance Minister Peter Bethlenfalvy wrote to LCBO Chair Carmine Nigro."The Government of Ontario is making similar commitments with our own advertising spending, helping to provide even more support for Ontario jobs and promote Ontario culture."Canada\'s media industry has gone through incredible upheaval over the past decade or more. That said, there is still an audience for news that informs us what is happening in our country, our province and our hometowns with a local point of view. You don\'t get that by spending your entire advertising budget with organizations based in California. You get that by supporting quality local journalism by advertising with the publishers making the investment in your own community. Premier Doug Ford\'s bold move is not only a welcome one, it\'s also a move that should be emulated by Prime Minister Justin Trudeau across the federal government and by provincial and municipal governments across the country.', ' Ontario\'s Ford government will direct one-quarter of its advertising budget toward news publishers in Canada\'s largest province, a targeted boost for a major domestic industry facing unprecedented pressure from internationally owned technology giants. That should amount to about $25 million in advertising each year going to Ontario publishers, including Postmedia Network Inc., which owns National Post, the Toronto Sun, Ottawa Citizen and community papers in the province."This is important. Everyone understands the value of journalism and a free press and its criticality to Canada and to democracy," said Andrew MacLeod, Postmedia\'s president and chief executive officer."I\'m certainly extremely grateful to the leadership of Premier (Doug) Ford and his team. My hope is this will serve as an example, a North Star, not just for other provincial governments, but for the federal government and for major corporations."In a letter, sent to Metrolinx (the public transit Crown corporation), the Ontario Lottery Gaming Corporation, the Ontario Cannabis Retail Corporation and the Liquor Control Board of Ontario, Ontario Finance Minister Peter Bethlenfalvy asks the government agencies to have the policy implemented by Sept. 3."Our government believes strongly in the importance of supporting and promoting Ontariomade products, services and workers," Bethlenfalvy\'s letter says. The initiative is in addition to the Progressive Conservative government\'s Building Ontario Businesses Initiative, which uses government procurement spending to support Ontario businesses, the Ontario Made Manufacturing Investment Tax Credit and initiatives aimed at boosting sales of Ontario-made beer and wine. Supporting workers"In addition to these actions, we believe there\'s a compelling opportunity to leverage the advertising spends of Ontario\'s major government agencies to support Ontario workers and content," the letter says. Ontario\'s major government agencies spend more than $100 million each year on advertising."These significant advertising budgets should help support Ontario-based publishers and the Ontario-based workers creating local news content for people in our province," the letter says. Publications eligible for the government advertising must be designated "Qualified Canadian Journalism Organizations" by the federal Canada Revenue Agency and must be Ontario-based corporations, trusts or partnerships."The Government of Ontario is making similar commitments with our own advertising spending, helping to provide even more support for Ontario jobs and promote Ontario culture," the letter says. MacLeod said the initiative is something the publishing industry has been lobbying for with the Ontario government and other governments in Canada, including the federal government, and that it "didn\'t make sense" that advertising dollars, paid for by taxpayers, were going to Google and Facebook."As I\'ve said countless times, the single biggest challenge facing our industry is that 90 per cent of the digital advertising budgets flow to foreign platforms," MacLeod said. "This is the first major, material step where we\'re seeing a significant institution, the province of Ontario, allocating a material portion of their spend on Ontario publishers, which supports Ontario journalism, Ontario jobs and the Ontario economy."Companies, including Postmedia, will need to wait to figure out just how much money they could get and what it will mean, MacLeod said."It\'s a hugely meaningful moment for our industry, certainly from an Ontario perspective, and to the extent that it serves as a beacon or a catalyst for other provincial governments and for the federal government to do the same," MacLeod said."What does it mean for Postmedia? I think time will tell. But we\'re one of the larger players, and we should have a meaningful pro rata portion of that based on the audiences that we reach in Ontario."The directive will be reviewed quarterly, the letter says. If it is not working to meet the objectives of "promoting local content and culture and supporting Ontario jobs," the government notes it may withdraw the funding directive. Postmedia, the largest newspaper company in Canada, saw its revenues drop to $97.3 million for the three-month period ending Feb. 29, 2024. Representative_Docs: [' Trump tariffs, a dearth of doctors, affordability anxieties. Ontario\'s snap winter campaign officially kicked off Wednesday with the major party leaders pushing competing narratives to define the Feb. 27 vote. Progressive Conservative Leader Doug Ford, trying to win his third majority government, was in Windsor against the backdrop of the Ambassador Bridge, railing against U.S. President Donald Trump\'s threatened 25 per cent tariffs on Canadian goods."I\'m asking the people for a strong, stable four-year mandate to do whatever it takes to protect Ontario," said Ford, who, despite already having a legislative majority, triggered a vote 15 months early that Elections Ontario says will cost $189 million. New Democratic Leader Marit Stiles was in Toronto\'s Regent Park to emphasize how "unaffordable" life has become since the Tories took office in 2018."People are leaving our province, forced out of communities they grew up in. Young people are losing hope. Seniors are ending up homeless. It\'s tough out there." said Stiles, noting unemployment has risen on Ford\'s watch. Liberal Leader Bonnie Crombie was in Barrie with local candidate Dr. Rose Zacharias, the former president of the Ontario Medical Association, to put a spotlight on the fact that 2.5 million people in the province don\'t have a doctor."We\'re launching our tour here in Barrie because 55,000 people residing in this area don\'t have access to a family doctor," said Crombie, sporting a white cap with the slogan "Real Leaders Fix Healthcare" that countered Ford\'s blue anti-Trump "Canada Is Not For Sale" hat. Green Leader Mike Schreiner, who was in Guelph, said "this election is a referendum on Doug Ford\'s poor track-record of the past seven years."In Windsor, where Ford unveiled his campaign vehicle - an RV emblazoned with his photo and the slogan "Protect Ontario" that press gallery wags immediately christened "the Winter-bago" - the Tory leader said the Trump threat will loom even if the president doesn\'t impose 25 per cent tariffs on Saturday."Ontario won\'t start a fight with the U.S., but you better believe we\'ll be ready to win one," he said as an icy wind blew over the Detroit River from across the border and a smattering of protesters from a teachers\' union rallied nearby. Ford pledged to spend "tens of billions" in economic supports to fight tariffs if necessary, similar to the fight against COVID-19."You may not always agree with me, and that\'s OK, but my record is clear," he said, appealing to voters leaning toward his rivals."There\'s experience on one side with the PC Party and zero experience with the other three parties."Asked about his alcohol sales expansion costing taxpayers an additional $612 million, Ford said he had no regrets."I believe the people should have a choice and the convenience if they want to grab a beer," added the PC leader, who does not drink alcohol."What I\'m happy about is convenience stores are making a little more money, they\'re hiring more people," he told reporters in the New Democrat-held riding of Windsor West. Ford\'s opponents say the additional expense proves the booze deal was botched and that he\'s not up to the job of going head-to-head with Trump on trade issues. Stiles, whose campaign slogan is "On Your Side," mocked the Tory leader\'s deal-making prowess."He wants us to hire him to be our negotiator with Trump. Doug Ford our negotiator? Is he kidding? Over and over, he makes bad deals for Ontarians," she said, pointing to the Ontario Place redevelopment when "Doug Ford got taken to the cleaners by a foreign corporation."In a rally with NDP MPPs and candidates at the Daniels Spectrum community art centre in Regent Park, Stiles also attacked Crombie, accusing the Liberal leader of making a right turn away from predecessors like former premier Kathleen Wynne."Today\'s Liberal leader would be right at home as a cabinet minister in Doug Ford\'s government. Bonnie Crombie doesn\'t want to get rid of Doug Ford - she wants to be Doug Ford," she quipped in the NDP-held riding. After governing for almost 15 years between 2003 and 2018, the Grits have been unable to win enough seats to obtain official party status in the past two elections."There will probably always be an Ontario Liberal party ... I think they\'re going to be in the repair shop for a few more years," said Stiles. In Tory-held Barrie, Crombie countered that the New Democrats have failed to hold the Tories accountable as the Official Opposition."They\'ve also had seven years to make a difference and make a change - they haven\'t gotten it done," she said, conceding she\'s "a different kind of Liberal" with a business background before she was a MP and the three-term mayor of Mississauga."I understand government and I know how to get things done."But Crombie reiterated "this isn\'t a necessary election" and said Ford is scrambling to "outrun an RCMP investigation" in the Tories\' $8.28-billion Greenbelt land swap scandal. At Queen\'s Park, Ontario chief electoral officer Greg Essensa said it will cost Elections Ontario $189 million to conduct the first winter vote in the province since 1981.Essensa, who needs to hire 55,000 workers to staff some 7,000 polling stations in all 124 provincial ridings, urged anyone looking for a temporary job during the writ period to apply at Elections Ontario\'s employment portal. With weather a factor at this time of year, the chief electoral officer said "contingency" planning has begun to ensure Ontarians are able to exercise their franchise even if there are blizzards across the province. Some 10.8 million people are eligible to vote, including the estimated 81,000 who are homeless. They can use the address of the shelter they stay at when they cast their ballots. Parties are allowed to spend $10.8 million on their campaigns. Schreiner, meanwhile, blasted "Ford\'s wasteful spending that only benefits wealthy land speculators and fossil fuel giants like Enbridge, all while ripping off everyday Ontarians who are struggling to make ends meet."People deserve better than Doug Ford and this is our chance to turn things around for the many communities that feel abandoned by this government," he said.', ' Premier Doug Ford is sending voters to the polls 15 months early, with a snap election he says is needed to deal with the threat posed to Ontario\'s economy by U.S. President Donald Trump and his avowed tariffs on Canadian exports. Here are some key things to know ahead of Wednesday\'s expected election call: BLAMING TRUMP Even before Trump took office this month, Ford - with two majority Progressive Conservative governments under his belt - appeared to be itching for an early election. Speculation about an election before the next scheduled one, in June 2026, ran rampant last fall as Ford ruled out a late 2024 vote but refused to take 2025 off the table. Then came Trump\'s election in November and his inauguration in January, with his threat to slap 25 per cent tariffs on Canadian exports to the U.S. Such a move could cost up to 500,000 jobs in Ontario\'s export-driven economy, some officials estimate."Make no mistake about it, he\'s coming for us," the premier has warned. Ford, who has become something of a Captain Canada in recent weeks, appearing widely in American media to defend Canadian interests amid the Trump threat, now insists he needs a "clear mandate" to deal with four years of Trump\'s second presidency and the damaging fallout it could have on Ontario. CRITICS SEE CYNICISM Critics contend Ford doesn\'t need to call an early election, since he has a majority government and as premier already has the job of defending Ontario\'s interests."While our province faces a grave threat with half a million jobs at risk, Doug Ford sees an opportunity to fight for one job - his own," New Democrat leader Marit Stiles, the opposition leader at Queen\'s Park, said Friday."He thinks he can con Ontarians with an early election to escape his record - but we won\'t let him."Wednesday\'s election-call will come nearly two weeks after Ontario started mailing out $200 cheques to virtually every man, woman and child in the province, a roughly $3-billion mass mail-out of money that Ford promised last fall to help Ontarians cope with higher costs including from the federal Liberal carbon tax. Opponents have categorized the move as an attempt to buy voters with their own money. Ford\'s PCs have a commanding majority in the Ontario legislature, holding about two-thirds of its seats."It does seem opportunistic. Like many people, I suspect, I\'m skeptical of the rationale of needing a new mandate," said Matt Farrell, a political science instructor at Fanshawe College in London."What more of a mandate does he need? He has a 50-seat lead in the legislature now."WHAT \'S NEXT - Coming off a "super-caucus" strategy meeting with PC candidates Saturday, Ford will visit Ontario\'s lieutenant-governor on Wednesday to ask that the legislature be dissolved and the election writs issued, one for each riding in the province. That will trigger a 29-day campaign, with the election held Feb. 27 - one month after Trump has hinted his avowed tariffs could take effect, and 10 days before the federal Liberals choose a new leader for their fragile minority government to replace the departing Justin Trudeau as prime minister. A federal election is widely expected to follow soon after, with either the Liberal government falling sometime after the prorogued Parliament resumes March 24 or the new prime minister pulling the plug and sending voters to the polls. HISTORY ON THE LINE Ford is gunning for a third straight majority under his watch, something no Ontario premier has pulled off since 1959. Liberal premier Dalton McGuinty came oh-so close in 2011, finishing the election that year one seat shy of three straight majorities. Between them, John Robarts and Bill Davis managed three consecutive PC majorities ending in 1971. But for the last majority hat trick under one premier, you have to go back to Leslie Frost who led his PCs to victory in 1951, \'55 and \'59.THE MAGIC NUMBERS Ford\'s PCs hold 79 seats in the 124-seat legislature, the opposition NDP 28 and the Liberals nine. The Green party has two seats and six members sit as independents. A party needs to win 63 seats for a simple majority, but more is better since the speaker of the legislature usually comes from the ruling party, reducing its voting strength by one. THE COST Another important number to consider? The actual cost of sending Ontarians to the polls. The province\'s last general election in 2022 cost taxpayers $145.3 million, but the tab is expected to be higher this time factoring in increased costs and the run-up in inflation since then. THE ISSUES Ford is trying to frame the election as a referendum on which leader and party is best suited to deal with Trump and the billions of dollars the U.S. president\'s avowed tariffs could cost Ontario. Watch for the other parties to zero in on government baggage ranging from homelessness and the affordability crisis many Ontarians are feeling, the 2.5 million residents of the province with no family doctor and a criminal investigation by the RCMP into a controversial plan to remove land for new housing from the protected Greenbelt near Toronto, a land swap the Tories moved to reverse following a public and political uproar. Heading into the election, a Leger poll conducted for Postmedia and published last week suggested affordability concerns are the top issue, with 28 per cent of respondents ranking the cost of living as the most important issue in their community. That was far ahead of the No. 2 issue, health care, at 12 per cent, and the economy, which was a top priority for 11 per cent. Five per cent ranked U.S. relations, including Trump tariffs, as the most important issue. AREN\'T ELECTION DATES FIXED? Yes and no. Ontario has a fixeddate election law, requiring one to be held every four years, but that doesn\'t stop the lieutenant-governor from dissolving the legislature at the request of the premier. Under the law, Ontario\'s next election date would have been June 4, 2026.THE RISK The last time an Ontario premier with a majority called an early election, it backfired badly. Liberal premier David Peterson, high in the polls three years into a majority, called an election in 1990 with economic storm clouds on the horizon. What looked to be a summer sleeper for the Liberals quickly turned into a nightmare. Beset by single-issue protest groups and suspicion the Liberals were trying to bag another victory before tough times hit, the party lost the election - and Peterson his London seat - to Bob Rae\'s New Democrats, who battled a brutal recession that followed. There\'s always a risk voters could punish Ford for the early election, returning his government in a weakened position, said Laura Stephenson, chair of the political science department at Western University. THE REWARD While there\'s always a risk in ending an otherwise stable majority, Farrell said the potential payoff for Ford outweighs the dangers. Calling an election now means Ford can catch the Liberals, under leader Bonnie Crombie, at a time when they\'re still rebuilding from severe election defeats in 2018 and 2022, Farrell said."The new Liberal leader has not really been defined yet for voters," he said. "It gives the PCs a chance to define the Liberal leader while being in a position of strength as an incumbent government."This election will be the first as party leader for both Crombie, who took the Liberal helm in December 2023, and for the NDP\'s Stiles, who took over from Andrea Horwath in February 2023.Even though federal and provincial politics are separate, the recent turmoil for Trudeau\'s Liberals could also affect how some voters see the Ontario Liberals, Farrell said. THE HORSE RACE Recent polling suggests Ford\'s PCs enter the starting gate with the election theirs to lose. The latest Leger survey of voter intentions, conducted Jan. 17 to 19, found Ford\'s PCs with the support of 46 per cent of respondents, to 22 per cent for Crombie\'s Liberals. When asked who they\'d vote for if an election was held today, 19 per cent of respondents said they\'d vote for the NDP. The survey results are considered accurate to within 3.08 per cent, plus or minus, 19 times out of 20. jbieman@postmedia.com', ' TORONTO - Premier Doug Ford plans to call a snap election next Wednesday and send Ontarians to the polls on Feb. 27, The Canadian Press reported Thursday. Two senior government sources said Ford recently made the decision for the rare winter election after waffling for months. The Canadian Press is not naming them so they can speak candidly about internal government deliberations. The election had been set for June 2026, but Ford has said he needs a new mandate in order to deal with four years of a Donald Trump presidency in the United States. He all but confirmed an imminent election earlier Thursday."I\'m asking for a mandate from the people of Ontario to make sure that we protect them," Ford said at an unrelated announcement."I really feel we\'re going to be investing billions and billions of dollars to protect the people, to protect communities and protect businesses here, and there\'s no more important group of people than the people of Ontario to give you a clear mandate to be able to invest into the people and businesses."His Progressive Conservative party plans to hold a "super caucus" event on Saturday to talk about the tariffs and "what\'s going on here in Ontario."The sources say the event is about election preparation. Ford said he can be both premier of the province and campaign as leader of the Progressive Conservatives. He still plans to head to Washington, D.C., twice in February to "make our case" to U.S. lawmakers to avoid tariffs. Ford has said he expects Trump tariffs to hit Ontario particularly hard, specifically the auto sector. He said Ontario could lose upwards of 500,000 jobs should Trump follow through on his 25-per-cent tariff threat. Opposition parties have said an early election is not necessary because they would support stimulus spending, and Ford - a premier with a majority government - already has a mandate to protect Ontario\'s interests."Today, Doug Ford has chosen himself over our province," Ontario Liberal Leader Bonnie Crombie said in a social media post Thursday evening."Recklessness over responsibility. His own political career, over the countless Ontario workers at risk of losing their jobs at this time of record instability."Prior to the looming trade war with the United States, the opposition parties were positioning housing and health care, particularly a shortage of family doctors, as two main campaign issues. Both are still likely to get a lot of attention amid tariff talk. All parties have been preparing for the possibility of an early election since last spring. At the time, Ford was asked if he was speeding up the expansion of beer and wine sales to corner stores, at a cost of $225 million, in order to plan for an early vote. He refused to rule it out. Election speculation ramped up in the fall as Ford continued to duck questions, at one point saying he would not hold one "this year," meaning in 2024. He did not then provide a reason for leaving the door open to a 2025 contest. Opposition politicians suggested Ford was being opportunistic and wanted an election before a federal vote. Polls had Pierre Poilievre and his Conservative party well ahead and poised to crush Prime Minister Justin Trudeau\'s Liberal government. Ontario has a long history of electing governments of a different political stripe than the one in Ottawa. The opposition, led by NDP Leader Marit Stiles, the Liberals\' Crombie and Green Party Leader Mike Schreiner, also accused Ford of trying to get an election in before the conclusion of an RCMP probe into the government\'s decision to open up parts of the protected Greenbelt to development. Ford had walked back the Greenbelt plan, but it caused turmoil internally, leading to the resignations of then-housing minister Steve Clark and his chief of staff. In the provincial government\'s fall economic statement, Ford announced a $3-billion plan to send out $200 cheques in early 2025 to every Ontario taxpayer and their children. The premier framed it as a way to help Ontarians amid an ongoing affordability crisis, but the opposition said it was nothing more than a vote-buying scheme ahead of an election. After Trump won the U.S. election in November, Ford took centre stage among the country\'s premiers as they pressured Ottawa to prepare for the incoming president. Trump pledged to lay 25 per cent tariffs on Canadian goods, a promise that has yet to come to fruition, though the threat remains. Trudeau\'s Liberal government imploded in mid-December after his finance minister, Chrystia Freeland, quit. A few weeks later, Trudeau told the country he would prorogue Parliament and step aside as Liberal leader while the party undertook a leadership race. A new federal Liberal leader is set to be chosen March 9 and federal opposition parties have promised to trigger an election if Parliament returns as scheduled on March 24.That leaves Ford with a narrow window to squeeze in a provincial election ahead of a likely federal campaign. It was only recently that Ford publicly offered a justification for considering an early election, saying that he needed a "mandate" from the people in order to spend billions of dollars should the threatened tariffs materialize.']

Representative_Docs: [' They lined up in the middle of the night, braving snow squalls and frigid temperatures, not for sought-after concert tickets or a Boxing Day doorcrasher deal, but just for a chance to get a family doctor. That was the scene in Walkerton weeks ago, where the imminent arrival of a new doctor in the midwestern Ontario community attracted a crowd of more than 1,000 people; the first 500 getting a doctor, the remainder put on a wait list for another expected to arrive later this year."What we\'re seeing is more than a crisis, it\'s a catastrophe in many communities," said Dr. Dominik Nowak, president of the Ontario Medical Association, a group that represents the province\'s 43,000 physicians."It\'s not the first time something like this has happened in Ontario. Across the province nearly one in four people are without a family doctor."In a provincial election whose early days were typified by toughtalk about U.S. President Donald Trump\'s avowed tariffs on Canadian goods and general cost-ofliving concerns, Nowak and others are urging voters to make the family doctor crisis a ballot-box issue. More than 2.5 million Ontarians are without a family doctor, the all-important entry-point for patients into the publicly funded health care system. That number is expected to balloon to 4.4 million by 2026, as family doctors retire or leave the field in the coming years, the OMA estimates. In Windsor, the OMA says 27 doctors are needed for 34,000 unattached patients."We need this to be an election issue," said Dr. Jobin Varughese, president of the Ontario College of Family Physicians, a non-profit group that represents more than 18,000 family physicians and medical students in the province."Ontarians want family doctors. We don\'t want what happened in Walkerton, with people lining up for hours for a family doctor, to happen in other communities. But it really could in the current situation."Whichever party forms the government on Feb. 27 should revisit the fees Ontario\'s health insurance plan pays family doctors, which has been stagnant for more than a decade, Nowak said."That\'s one of the main reasons we see family practices closing up shop or doctors retiring with no one to replace them," Nowak said, adding the fees paid to doctors sometimes aren\'t enough to run a practice."Our funding models are decades out of date and they haven\'t kept up with what patients need."But funding is only one factor. The OMA wants to see the provincial government establish more team-based clinics where family doctors and other healthcare providers including nurses, physiotherapists, social workers and occupational therapists can work together."Only around 30 per cent of practices have that kind of support," Nowak said, adding this comprehensive, collaborative model also attracts new graduates to work in family medicine."There\'s been a stagnation of not just modernizing funding models, but building and expanding these teams over the last decade or so."A provincial government that is serious about solving the family doctor crisis would also reduce the administrative burden on physicians, who are spending approximately 19 hours a week on paperwork, on top of the time they spend seeing patients, Varughese said. Access to artificial intelligence note-taking software and the development of a centralized referral system, which would cut down on the time family doctors spend chasing down specialist appointments for their patients, would help, he said. Fixing the system family doctors work within will pay off, Varughese said."Family doctors find joy in their work, when they\'re not burdened by the system or having administrative hurdles that hold them up or devalue the work that they do," Varughese said. "The Ontario College of Family Physicians has solutions and people who are willing to help. We want to get to the point where every Ontarian has access to a family physician." WHERE THE BIG THREE PARTIES STAND LIBERALSThe Ontario Liberals have pledged to educate, attract and retain 3,100 family doctors in the province if elected, ensuring everyone in Ontario has a primary care physician within four years. Calling fixing family medicine the "single most important priority" if it forms government, the Liberals are pledging to bring in new domestic and internationally trained family doctors. The Liberals are also promising to improve and expand access to team-based clinics and modernize family medicine by eliminating the use of fax machines and making appointments available on evenings and weekends. The Liberals\' plan also includes ending the practice of penalizing patients and doctors when patients seek care at walk-in clinics. NEW DEMOCRATSThe Ontario NDP said Sunday it will be releasing more details in the coming days, but have advocated for increased funding for primary health care teams, home care and hospital care. Among other pledges, the party is promising to connect every Ontarian to a family doctor or nurse practitioner by recruiting more health care professionals into primary care teams and increasing residency seats and licensing opportunities for internationally educated doctors."Under Doug Ford\'s Conservatives, people are left waiting for primary care, emergency rooms have been shuttered, and for-profit health care has exploded," NDP Leader Marit Stiles said in a statement last month, adding "improving access will take political leadership that has so far been absent in our province."PROG. CON SERVATIVESDoug Ford\'s Progressive Conservative government, on the eve of the election call, announced $1.4 billion in new funding to connect two million more people to family doctors and primary care teams within four years. The amount is in addition to a previous $400 million earmarked for primary care by the Ford government. The funding will be used to implement the plan created by Ontario\'s Primary Care Action Team, a panel led by former federal health minister Jane Philpott. As part of that pre-election announcement, the PC government said they planned to introduce legislation to outline the standards people in Ontario can expect when accessing primary care.jbeiman@postmedia.com HOW MANY FAMILY DOCTORS DO WE NEED? ESTIMATED FAMILY DOCTOR SHORTAGE AS OF 2022, BY COMMUNITY', ' Retired family physician Marlene Spruyt, the Green Party candidate for Lanark-Frontenac-Kingston, remembers a time when she called up a home care nurse for a dying patient. "We delivered palliative care to a woman who was blind, and she got to stay at home and die," she says. "Now, you can\'t deliver that quality of care."For the 2.5 million Ontarians without a family doctor (up from 1.8 million in 2020), Spruyt\'s memory sounds like myth. But that level of care could return, if only leaders would summon up the political will. Ontarians are now being asked to choose a new leader. Progressive Conservative leader Doug Ford called a snap election for Feb. 27 in response to the threat of U.S. tariffs 16 months before an election was due. But according to a recent Nanos survey, nearly 30 per cent of voters say health care concerns will dictate how they cast their ballots. The Nanos poll shows 28 per cent of voters favour the Liberals on health care while 26 per cent support Ford. The NDP trails at 21 per cent. Perhaps most damning of all is the Nanos finding that one in five Ontarians don\'t trust any party on health care. Ontarians know just how precarious the health system is. For two decades, governments of all stripes have failed to address the demands of an exploding, aging population. The Ontario Medical Association predicts that by 2026 - that\'s next year - 4.4 million people won\'t have a family doctor. The OMA says Ontario needs 3,500 new family doctors now. It gets worse. Close to 40 per cent of family doctors are nearing retirement. Poor pay combined with runaway inflation make running the business of family practice financially unsustainable. The falling number of medical school seats per capita means a shortage of doctors coming down the pipeline. And that\'s just the family doctor crisis. The province also needs to fund new hospitals, maintain existing ones, and pay for seniors\' long-term care. Addressing health care is a gargantuan task, but Ford\'s majority government has had seven years to fix the mess. Last year, the Ministry of Health infuriated doctors by stating that the recruitment and retention of Ontario physicians was "not a major concern."In 2024, the federal government transferred $3.1 billion to Ontario for health care. Last fall, Ford recruited former federal Liberal health minister Jane Philpott to implement her Primary Care Action Plan. But this anemic, late-in-the-day proposal calls for just $1.8 billion to connect two million Ontarians to 305 vaguely defined primary care teams in a school-board type model based on residential postal codes. Her plan emphasizes workforce retention and easing administrative burden but is sketchy on financial details. It also adds 500 new medical school seats by 2028.The Greens, who boast only two MPPs, present a bolder platform. They say they\'ll recruit 3,500 family doctors. According to Marlene Spruyt, this plan represents a stark contrast from the PCs. Spruyt cites the various ways Ford has failed to shore up health care, including lost savings from breaking a contract with The Beer Store. For a guy who says he doesn\'t drink, she calls his beer fixation "bizarre.""What has Doug Ford done right?" she asks. Spruyt says municipalities shouldn\'t have to fund health care. She wants the government to pay half the cost to build hospitals in towns like Bracebridge, where rich donors are scarce. Nobody asks citizens to chip in for a new police car, she adds. For her part, NDP Leader Marit Stiles has pledged to spend $4 billion over four years to bring in 3,500 family doctors and 15,000 nurses to work in teams. The party\'s health critic France Gelinas represents the northern riding of Nickel Belt, where 30,000 residents lack a family doctor. She says the Ford government has knowingly allowed conditions to deteriorate, and adds that Ford\'s government listens to investors, while the NDP listens to front-line staff. Gelinas says the NDP respects family physicians."They\'ve been providing quality primary care for a very long time. They need to be paid fairly."She\'s also frustrated that although Sudbury\'s Northern Ontario School of Medicine can increase its capacity from 56 to 100 undergraduate seats "right now," the government won\'t release the funding yet. As for Bonnie Crombie\'s Liberals, they have also vowed to increase the number of physicians, promising to pair every Ontarian with a family doctor-led team of allied health professionals by spending $3.1 billion to "attract and retain 3,100 family doctors" by 2029. They will double medical school spots, entice 2,400 aging doctors to delay retirement and invest $250 million to recruit 650 doctors who\'ve decamped elsewhere for better pay and less paperwork back to family practice. Liberal Adil Shamji, the MPP for Don Valley East who, he says, is "the only elected physician" at Queen\'s Park says the government\'s track record speaks for itself, with lukewarm promises coming years too late. He says Ford found money for everything but health care, including $3.2 billion - which could pay for the Liberal health platform and then some - on $200 taxpayer rebates. Shamji says Ontarians pay taxes for family doctors and worries that to cut costs the current government is diluting the definition of primary care by trying to "convince Ontarians that if they have a pharmacist who can prescribe for minor ailments, that counts as ... primary care, and it doesn\'t."These juicy promises from political parties still trailing the incumbent in the polls sound like a Christmas wish list for patients and doctors alike. Adam Stewart, who practices comprehensive family medicine in Madoc, a rural town halfway between Toronto and Ottawa, believes that money is the priority. He sits on the board of the OMA\'s Section on General and Family Practice. Only 65 per cent of family doctors are left in comprehensive, longitudinal practices offering cradle to grave care. They\'re incurring "20, maybe 30 per cent increases" in overhead from post-pandemic inflation balanced against one per cent annual fee increases. Stewart says government needs to bump up family doctor compensation to be in line with BC and other provinces. He also wants Ontario to recognize family doctors as specialists in looking after patients from birth to death. They\'re ready to assume higher patient loads by leading multi-professional teams. Stewart also has some more unconventional recommendations. Put the joy back into medicine, he says, by providing doctors with AI technology for scribes. Implement a centralized referral system for rapid access to specialists and MRIs. These reforms are crucial, says Stewart. "If things don\'t get fixed," he says, if they continue down the same sad trajectory, he might have to leave comprehensive practice, too. Merrilee Fullerton, a retired family doctor and two-time Progressive Conservative MPP from Kanata-Carleton calls the Ford government\'s $1.8-billion offer "a hail Mary pass."Fullerton says too often, governments laud shiny baubles, like AI, that are distractions from the fact that family doctors are the glue that holds the system together. She resigned her seat in 2023 because of "tremendous frustration" with the government\'s lackadaisical approach to health care. Fullerton wants policymakers, bureaucrats, and politicians to think ahead. She calls making hasty health care election promises, then forgetting them till the next election cycle "irresponsible."In April 2005, faced with family doctor shortages, Liberal premier Dalton McGuinty announced new Family Health Teams to serve 2.5 million Ontarians. But when family doctors tried to join those teams, McGuinty and his successor Kathleen Wynne froze the funding. It was too expensive. Some lucky Ontarians got team-based care, while millions more didn\'t and even fewer do now. McGuinty also imposed the Health Premium tax in 2004, a levy of up to $900 that Ontarians still pay annually. There\'s nothing new here. Then, as now, Ottawa injected cash into Ontario\'s coffers. Then, as now, governments promised primary care teams to solve provincial health care woes. Will much-touted team funding be frozen again?Not one Ontario political party in the past 20 years has demonstrated the grit needed to fix health care. The Progressive Conservatives still lead the Liberals by 15 percentage points. Barring an electoral miracle, Ford seems destined to be a three-time premier. Patients are tired of not having family doctors to give their newborns their childhood shots, and are tired of waiting months to see the orthopedic surgeon while their knees crumble. Doctors are tired of working longer, harder, faster to keep their patients healthy with shrinking resources.', ' The sprawling second-floor office, located above a pharmacy on the city\'s main street, at one time was home to eight doctors serving the busy neighbourhood. But the physicians, with large patient rosters, were burning out and six were ready to retire, but couldn\'t find anyone willing to take over the practice. Two years ago, they all left, the clinic shuttered and 8,000 patients suddenly found themselves adrift - joining about two million others across the province with no access to a family doctor. It\'s not a problem unique to Kingston - many communities across the province are grappling with a lack of primary care - and it has emerged as a key issue in Ontario\'s Feb. 27 election. The opposition parties have hammered the PCs for being in power for seven years as the situation they inherited worsened, which even the government acknowledged has taken too long to fix and left too many without a family doctor. But what has happened here since that clinic closed is a new model that has been able to attract physicians and taken thousands off the wait-list, a model that appears to have the support of the PCs, Liberals and NDP.That same Princess Street office reopened last summer as a "primary care home," as proposed by Dr. Jane Philpott, a former federal Liberal health minister and dean of the medical school at Queen\'s recently hired by the PC government to help fix the province\'s health problems. Her vision, outlined in her 2024 book "Health for All" - which she calls the periwinkle model - guarantees primary care for everyone based on their postal code, much like families being assigned a local school based on their address. Two days before the provincial election campaign kicked off last week, the government and Philpott announced funding with a promise of primary care for all Ontarians by 2029, a total of $1.8 billion for every Ontarian to have a family doctor or primary care team within four years. The government, however, says two million Ontarians need a physician, which is based on work by organizations like the Canadian Institute for Health Information, but the Ontario Medical Association says the number is 2.5 million and could rise to 4.4 million by 2026.Last fall, Philpott spoke at the Liberal policy convention, and Leader Bonnie Crombie announced Thursday that if elected, she would spend $3 billion over four years to connect everyone with a family doctor. On Friday, NDP Leader Marit Stiles unveiled a $4.05-billion, four-year plan to get all Ontarians access to a doctor or nurse practitioner, pledging more family health teams. Philpott\'s model, based on similar ones in the Netherlands and the United Kingdom, ideally provide patients access to care seven days a week, taking pressure of emergency rooms and steering them away from walk-in clinics. They are treated by practitioners they know, and who know their histories; medical records are in one place, and once a full network of sites are in place, no one would worry about finding a family doctor if they move. The Midtown Kingston Health Home opened last July, two years after a proposal by various health-care partners in the city obtained funding from the provincial government. At the health home, each family doctor works in a team with a nurse practitioner, sharing "provider pod" offices, with a host of in-demand services on site - diabetes care, COPD care, social worker, family health educator - mostly for those within the K7M postal code. Community clinics for well baby care, sexual health and quick STI testing are open to all. Practical assistance workers help patients who might need help co-ordinating insulin injections for their child while at school, or finding housing, or applying for a birth certificate. It\'s hoping to secure funding to add occupational therapists, physiotherapists, mental health case management and footcare, to make it more of a one-stop community hub for patients."The doctors, they were asking me all kinds of questions about my history and this and that, and I was just blown away, because my (previous) doctor would not engage with anything you would have asked him, and I always felt rushed," said lifelong Kingston resident Mario Borsato, 56, now a patient of the health home. He and several of his family members had sought care at the original clinic for 20 years, and found themselves without a doctor for two years, so he knows the struggles of those who are still looking."If you don\'t have your health, you don\'t have nothing," he added. "And our family care (in the province) has gone down the tubes."About 4,400 residents in the K7M postal code were on the wait-list through Health Care Connect, but it is estimated the actual need is double that. So far, the health home has rostered 1,418 patients and - and treated another 1,535 through its various clinics - and expects to have 4,000 patients signed up by the end of March and 8,000 patients by March 2026.Winn Studsrud, a patient of the original clinic, was directed to the health home after seeking help with a prescription, but it wasn\'t until later that she realized she\'d been taken on by a family doctor there, even though she doesn\'t live in the postal code."I freaking started crying," she said. "I couldn\'t stop smiling, actually. And I just kept saying \'thank you Lord, thank you Lord.\' So honestly, it\'s like a miracle."Dr. Mary Rowland, clinical lead, calls the health home "a really nice blend" and likens it to a secondary school, where "this school has the IB program, this school has French Immersion. We have a catchment, and we have these specialized programs for more supports for particular populations."Dr. Eileen Nicolle, who moved with her family from Toronto to Kingston to be a part of the health home, said "you can provide the most holistic care and also take the time you need to see people ... I think if you take a more long-term approach, there\'s very much a cost saving and also a time saving because those problems that you don\'t deal with right up front, they come back."Currently, the clinic is open five days a week with evening clinic hours, and has managed to attract five physicians so far, with one to come, plus locums, as well as three nurse practitioners. Staff are on salary, have flexible hours and a team-centred approach. Doctors like it because they don\'t have to run a business as they would setting up their own practice. They work more reasonable hours, and can leave when they want, "but they don\'t" because it\'s such an attractive set up, said Meghan O\'Leary, director of clinical services for Kingston Community Health Centres. Nurse practitioner Edward Cho was the first hire, and saw the patient roster grow - though initially there was some upset as those from the old clinic weren\'t necessarily able to re-register. Cho values being paired with a doctor, because "there are more opportunities for patients to get followups" in a timely manner."I\'m not worried about my patients" when away, he added. "I always know they\'re covered. If there are urgent issues, I know they\'re well taken care of ... having two eyes, rather than one, is always a good thing."Personally, he said the way the interdisciplinary model works gives him the "perfect work-life balance. I\'m not stressed. I go home knowing that my inbox is taken care of, and I won\'t come back to 10 million messages. I finish all my charting on time."For Nicolle, working with a male nurse practitioner gives patients choice. "Maybe they want to see a female for their Pap smear. Or maybe the men would rather see Ed for certain things. So it gives you a bit of diversity within the practice."Research on team-based care has been shown to benefit patients\' health and means a drop in hospitalizations and visits to the ER. Patients report higher levels of satisfaction and care, and health-care providers report higher job satisfaction and are less likely to burn out, says Jennifer Rayner, director of policy and research at the Alliance for Healthier Communities. Raisa Deber, professor emeritus at the Institute of Health Policy, Management and Evaluation at the University of Toronto, said there are a number of team-based models in the province, and there must be flexibility in the system because what works in a large, urban centre may not in a rural or remote area where it might be difficult to get additional services. Dr. Tara Kiran, family physician and researcher at St. Michael\'s Hospital and the University of Toronto, works in a family health team that includes nurses, nurse practitioners, social workers, pharmacists and others, focusing on a vulnerable population. When more than one in five people in Canada don\'t have access to any primary care, with services varying by region, "we need to do things differently to try and even out the way services are provided ... so that we don\'t have the have and have-not, but rather, everybody has something."The periwinkle model does address that and needs to be evaluated to see if it does attract doctors and is able to better clear wait-lists."There is a bit of an experiment here, and we do need to learn from it," Kiran added. The Kingston model is part of a wider network that has a community board of governors, which is key, said Kate Mulligan, a professor at the Dalla Lana School of Public Health at the University of Toronto."If we\'re going to go to all the trouble of doing team-based primary care, which is the right next step, we shouldn\'t miss the opportunity to leverage the huge capacity that\'s there, to really connect that into our health care system," Mulligan said.']

Representative_Docs: [' By any reasonable metric, the Ford government deserves a failing grade for its handling of Ontario\'s housing crisis. This track record, however, does not appear to be harming the Progressive Conservatives in the polls, partly because other issues are more salient to voters, and partly because our crisis has gotten so large that young voters have come to believe they will never be able to afford a home, regardless of who is in power. Rather than a single crisis, Ontario\'s housing system faces a set of interlocking crises that share some common causes. First, there is a lack of deeply affordable housing for lower-income Ontarians. Four decades of underinvestment in non-profit and co-op housing, coupled with stagnant wages and Ontario Works and ODSP shelter allowances that have not kept up with rent inflation, have priced too many people out of the market. Homelessness has grown by 25 per cent in Ontario since 2022, and food bank use has hit record levels. Second is the rental crisis, though we have seen some relief in recent months, with rents on new leases falling 5 per cent in the last year. They remain, however, highly unaffordable to low- and middle-income workers. Finally, there\'s the home ownership crisis. When Doug Ford first took office in June 2018, it took 282 weeks of median wages to finance a 20 per cent down payment and the first five years of mortgage payments on a single-family home in Ontario. Today, it takes 327 weeks. The comparable figures for Alberta and Nova Scotia are 203 and 156 weeks, respectively. When Ford was first elected, more families moved to Ontario from other provinces than the other way around. Last year, however, 25,000 more people moved out of Ontario to other provinces than moved in. Young Ontarians are increasingly seeking opportunities elsewhere. The common cause of all three crises is population growth outpacing housing supply. Despite out-migration to other provinces, Ontario\'s population grew by 1.8 million over the past six years due to increased immigration targets and an international student boom, the latter resulting from colleges and universities massively increasing their international enrolments in response to the Ford government\'s domestic tuition freeze. In the previous six years, the province\'s population grew by less than 1 million. Ontario now has an estimated shortfall of 740,000 units. This figure understates the shortage, as the homes that have been built in Ontario in recent years have largely been one-bedroom condos and rental apartments, which naturally house fewer people than other forms of housing. Ramping up homebuilding to keep up with such rapid levels of population growth was a near-impossible task, one made more difficult through a combination of municipal delays, continued underinvestment in social housing, skyrocketing development charges and other fees on new housing, zoning rules preventing the building of family-friendly gentle density and a lack of competition in the residential development land market, which left land prices prohibitively expensive. The Ford government recognized many of these as problems and assembled a team of experts to draft the comprehensive Housing Affordability Task Force Report. The government also recognized that a growing population needs more housing, so it created a target to build 1.5 million homes and individual targets for 50 municipalities. These targets are proportional to the need created by accelerated population growth. However, the majority of the task force\'s recommendations have gone unheeded, and the lack of any requirement to adopt provincial targets in municipal planning has robbed those targets of their effectiveness. Even when the Ford government has recognized a problem, its solutions have largely been ineffective. Ford has been right to point out that municipal red tape is an issue, but beyond the incentives that the government\'s Building Faster Fund created, little progress has been made. Ford did make large reforms to development charges - only to reverse those changes in response to opposition from municipalities. The government\'s decision to open up more land for development, including by taking land out of the Greenbelt, not only led to substantial backlash from Ontarians but also triggered an RCMP investigation. In other housing policy areas, such as social housing, the Ford government has chosen not to act. In particular, it has fought against legalizing family-friendly density, calling attempts to allow for fourplexes as-of-right a "massive mistake." Earlier in this election campaign, Ford was endorsed onstage by Oakville Mayor Rob Burton. Burton praised Ford for not legalizing fourplexes and for not increasing height limits near transit stations. Ford has been consistent in allowing municipalities to set these rules for themselves, even though such rules amount to the kind of red tape Ford rails against. The opposition parties are advocating for a different approach. The Liberals, New Democrats and Greens are all calling for increased legalization of family-friendly density. The NDP is also advocating for a return of the provincial government to the non-profit and co-op housing space, setting a target of 300,000 new permanently affordable rental homes. It\'s an ambitious target, though it\'s unclear how any government could achieve it, and the NDP has not provided an estimate as to what such a program might cost. Ontario has never built 30,000 such homes in any single year, let alone for 10 consecutive years. Even if the province could keep the cost of each home under $350,000, that would still entail more than $100 billion in spending over a decade. Given the increasing cost pressures our health-care system is under, such high levels of spending seem unattainable. Both the Liberals and the Greens are advocating for eliminating development charges on most forms of housing, which would substantially help to bring down purchase prices. However, neither party has indicated how it would ensure that municipalities would be "made whole" and still have the funds needed to pay for infrastructure. Development charge reform is badly needed, but any replacement model must be fiscally sustainable. Unfortunately, no party is offering substantial reforms to the availability of residential development land, which is unsurprising, given how contentious an issue it is with the public. However, given that land is often the single-largest expense in building a home, any housing affordability agenda is incomplete without a plan to lower the cost of development land. There is a belief that making available just enough land for development is sufficient; however, this ensures a lack of competition in the land market and creates the conditions for monopolization. Instead, we need to ensure that enough development land is available to create real competition in the land market. Adding residential development land does not require opening up the Greenbelt, nor should we open up land in areas prone to flooding or fires, as the most expensive home is the one that you need to build twice. But it does mean having some difficult conversations about how population growth creates a need to expand urban growth boundaries, as well as allowing for more flexibility to switch land use from industrial and commercial to residential. We need a proper debate on how to fix Ontario\'s overlapping housing crises. It\'s unfortunate that this election is failing to provide one. Both reports call for housing to be built within cities and communities - not in fields and forests - to save money, combat climate change and facilitate rental housing. The proposals also put the province directly at odds with the federal government's plans to promote new housing within existing cities and communities. For the first time in decades, Ottawa has signaled clearly to Canadians it is back in the housing business, committing $8.5 billion in new spending. Representative_Docs: [' Why is Doug Ford promising to send a $200 payment to every Ontarian? To put it bluntly, because he can. Ford made official what had been reported weeks ago that the fall economic statement will include a tax rebate - "Dougie Dollars" if you will."We\'re able to provide the relief because inflation has increased provincial sales tax revenues and because of the federal government\'s recent changes to their capital gains tax," Ford said. To give you an example of how inflation has increased the government\'s sales tax revenues, in fiscal year 2019-20, the first full year of the Ford government, sales tax revenue stood at $28.6 billion. Representative_Docs: [' Colleges in Ontario are in deep financial trouble, leading many of the once-booming institutions to make unprecedented cutbacks to programming and staffing levels in recent months. One of the biggest announcements came last week, when St. Lawrence College in Kingston said it would be cutting 55 programs - a 40-per-cent reduction. Soon after, Loyalist College in Belleville also announced it was cutting 24 programs and laying off 20 per cent of staff. They joined a growing list of Ontario colleges to announce drastic cuts in recent months. Those cuts have come in the form of program suspensions, staffing reductions and closures of physical campus space in the wake of the federal government\'s decision in early 2024 to cap the number of international students allowed in Canada. This policy change has led to a steep decline in international student enrolment at post-secondary institutions throughout the country, and is hitting Ontario colleges particularly hard. Glenn Vollebregt, president and CEO of St. Lawrence College in Kingston, said the change has led to an enrol- ment drop of about 5,000 students, most of them international. Instead of around 12,000 students, they project less than 7,000 will be enrolled by September. This translates to a revenue drop of nearly 70 per cent."That becomes a very difficult operating model for us," Vollebregt said."When you couple that with the fact we are the lowest funded college system in Canada, and we have the lowest tuition in Canada - when you put those two things together, we have a challenge."The steep decline in international student enrolment has led to extraordinary cuts throughout the entire college sector, and it\'s had major ripple effects on their operations as they\'ve come to rely on the tuition fees paid by non-domestic students to help keep them afloat. The Ontario Public Service Employees Union (OPSEU), which represents more than 45,000 college faculty and support staff at the province\'s 24 public colleges, pointed out there\'s been a series of other cuts at its facilities across Ontario. In January, Centennial College announced it would be suspending 49 programs, or 28 per cent of overall programing. College president and CEO Craig Stephenson said the institution was adapting to changes to the federal government\'s immigration policy that led to a drop in international student enrolments, which significantly impacted the college\'s financial standing. Also, Mohawk College will eliminate 127 positions, 20 per cent of its full- and part-time support staff. Sheridan College is suspending 40 programs and laying off staff. Fanshawe College is cutting 18 programs amid a $35-million deficit this year, which it anticipates will grow to a whopping $60 million deficit in 2026 due to the federal government\'s decision. Seneca College\'s Markham site and Algonquin College\'s Perth site are the first campuses to shutter entirely, effective January 2025 and August 2026, respectively. Each of those colleges attributed the cuts to changes to the federal government\'s immigration policy, but the union says it runs deeper than that. OPSEU says since 2010, provincial grants and revenues from private sources have remained relatively stable in other provinces, while provincial funding has shrunk by 28 per cent in Ontario."Not only has (Premier Doug) Ford walked away from post-secondary education, he\'s shifted the responsibility of financing our colleges, a public good, onto students and institutions," JP Hornick, president of OPSEU and faculty at George Brown College, said in a prepared statement."It\'s negligent, and a failed formula sinking the system." HOW MANY COLLEGES ARE IN ONTARIO, AND HOW MANY HAVE ANNOUNCED CUTS?There are 24 public colleges in Ontario. At least eight institutions have publicly announced cuts in some form, including reductions in programming, staffing or physical campus closures. Vollebregt said the issues were plaguing the entire system, and that it\'s been building for years."It wouldn\'t surprise me if you see an nnouncement every couple of weeks from here \'til March," he said. WHAT IS DRIVINGTHE CUTS AT ONTARIO COLLEGES?In January 2024, the federal government announced it would be capping the amount of international students allowed in Canada. At the time, Immigration, Refugees, and Citizenship Canada announced it would reduce the amount of permits for international students by 35 per cent over 2023.It said the policy change was in response to "rapid increases in the number of international students arriving in Canada" which putee on "housing, health pressure care and other services."The decision was cemented thisyear when it announced a further reduction in the intake cap, droppingit another 10 per cent from the 2024 target of 485,000. This year, it plans to issue a total of 437,000 study permits. WHEN DID THE PROBLEMS BEGIN FOR ONTARIO COLLEGES?While the funding challenges were exacerbated by policy changes at the federal level, the problem has been building for years."Colleges have been underfunded for over a decade," Vollebregt said. According to Colleges Ontario, the association which represents public colleges in Ontario, the provincial government provides the smallest per-capita funding of post-secondary education in the country, an issue the college sector has long lobbied the province to correct. It\'s been that way since at least 2012, Vollebregt said, and it was made worse with a tuition freeze in 2019. At that time, the province reduced tuition by 10 per cent, and it has been frozen at that rate ever since. The move was aimed at increasing the affordability of college and university for Ontario students to "help people get the training they need to get good-paying jobs."The government had good intentions, but Vollebregt says it leaves colleges in a tough spot when dealing funding in 2012 dollars, and expenses are in 2025."There\'s a gap there," he said. HOW HAV E COLLEGES DEALT WITH LOWER- THANAVERAGE FUNDINGP To make up for the gap, colleges have relied more heavily on international student tuition. A steep drop in international students means an even steeper drop in revenue. Without the extra revenue generated by international students, Vollebregt said colleges can Ino longer afford to offer certain programming. When deciding which programs to cut in Kingston, Brockville and Cornwall, officials considered three factors, he said. They asked whether the program was financially sustainable, what the projected enrolment would be, and whether it met a labour market need."The reality is, because we have a student population of 12,000 students and the revenue that\'s associated with that, we were able to subsidize those programs that were not financially sustainable on their own," he said."If you take away that income 1OW, with that drop, we had to reduce our program intake for programs that are not financially sustainable on their own."HOW ARE COLLEGES FUNDED?Post-secondary institutions in Ontario receive funding for domestic students through a mix of provincial funding and tuition fees. That funding ratio is complicated, Vollebregt said, but it\'s approximately 60 per cent government funding to 40 per cent tuition. They do not receive funding for international students, leading them to pay higher tuition rates. HOW MUCH TUITION DO INTERNATIONAL STUDENTS PAY?According to Statistics Canada, the number of international students enrolled in Canadian public post-secondary educational institutions more than doubled in a decade, rising from 142,200 in 2010-2011 to 388,800 in 2019-2020.StatsCan also says international undergraduates pay almost five times more on average in tuition fees than Canadian students. The average tuition fees of undergraduate Canadian students rose by 27.8 per cent in 2010-2011 to $6,580 in 2020-2021, while those for undergraduate international students almost doubled to $32,039."Because tuition fees and enrolments of international students are growing at a much faster pace than their Canadian counterparts, their overall contribution to total tuition revenues at Canadian universities has risen. This has helped to make up for the reduction of provincial funding in universities\' budgets for their operational activities," StatsCan said in a 2024 report. WHAT DOES THE SECTOR NEED IN ORDER TO G ET BACK TO NORMAL?OPSEU says an emergency infusion of $1.4 billion is needed to stabilize the college system. Vollebregt agreed that investment into the sector is necessary. He said across the province, colleges are reducing operations and program offerings to become more sustainable, but he argued it\'s counterintuitive since post-secondary education is \'an incredibly valuable investment for any government, when you consider that highly trained and motivated graduates drive industry and help grow the economy."But now, more than ever, the need to fund colleges has reached an all-time high. That\'s what the sector needs so it can get back on its feet, Vollebregt said."Rather than one specifc thing, it\'s really an investment into the college system," he said."We\'re looking for partners to invest into us by the provincial government so that we can deliver on the provincial economic agenda and provide the talent that our economy needs, our local communities need. In January, Centennial College announced it would be suspending 49 programs, or 28 per cent of overall programing. College president and CEO Craig Stephenson said the institution was adapting to changes to the federal government\'s immigration policy that led to a drop in international student enrolments, which significantly impacted the college\'s financial standing. Also, Mohawk College will eliminate 127 positions, 20 per cent of its full- and part-time support staff. Sheridan College is suspending 40 programs and laying off staff. Fanshawe College is cutting 18 programs amid a $35-million deficit this year, which it anticipates will grow to a whopping $60 million defi- statement."It\'s negligent, and a failed formula sinking the system."How many colleges are in Ontario, and how many have announced cuts?There are 24 public colleges in Ontario. At least eight institutions have publicly announced cuts in some form, including reductions in programming, staffing or physical campus closures. Vollebregt said the issues were plaguing the entire system, and that it\'s been building for years."It wouldn\'t surprise me if you see an announcement every couple of weeks from here \'til March," he said. What is driving the cuts at Ontario colleges?In January 2024, the federal government announced it would be capping the amount of international students allowed in Canada. At the time, Immigration, Refugees, and Citizenship Canada announced it would reduce the amount of permits for international students by 35 per cent over 2023.It said the policy change was in response to "rapid increases in the number of international students arriving in Canada" which put pressure on "housing, health care and other services."The decision was cemented this year when it announced a further reduction in the intake cap, dropping it another 10 per cent from the 2024 target of 485,000. This year, it plans to issue a total of 437,000 study permits. When did the problems begin for Ontario colleges?While the funding challenges were exacerbated by policy changes at the federal level, the problem has been building for years."Colleges have been underfunded for over a decade," Vollebregt said. According to Colleges Ontario, the association which represents public colleges in Ontario, the provincial government provides the smallest per-capita funding of post-secondary education in the country, an issue the college sector has long lobbied the province to correct. It\'s been that way since at least 2012, Vollebregt said, and it was made worse with a tuition freeze in 2019. At that time, the province reduced tuition by 10 per cent, and it has been frozen at that rate ever since. The move was aimed at increasing the affordability of college and university for Ontario students to "help people get the training they need to get good-paying jobs."The government had good intentions, but Vollebregt says it leaves colleges in a tough spot when deal- ing funding in 2012 dollars, and expenses are in 2025."There\'s a gap there," he said. How have colleges dealt with lower-than-average funding?To make up for the gap, colleges have relied more heavily on international student tuition. A steep drop in international students means an even steeper drop in revenue. Without the extra revenue generated by international students, Vollebregt said colleges can no longer afford to offer certain programming. When deciding which programs to cut in Kingston, Brockville and Cornwall, officials considered three factors, he said. They asked whether the program was financially sustainable, what the projected enrolment would be, and whether it met a labour market need."The reality is, because we have a student population of 12,000 students and the revenue that\'s associated with that, we were able to subsidize those programs that were not financially sustainable on their own," he said. "If you take away that income now, with that drop, we had to reduce our program intake for programs that are not financially sustainable on their own."How are colleges funded? Post-secondary institutions in Ontario receive funding for domestic students through a mix of provincial funding and tuition fees. That funding ratio is complicated, Vollebregt said, but it\'s approximately 60 per cent government funding to 40 per cent tuition. They do not receive funding for international students, leading them to pay higher tuition rates. How much tuition do international students pay?According to Statistics Canada, the number of international students enrolled in Canadian public post-secondary educational institutions more than doubled in a decade, rising from 142,200 in 20102011 to 388,800 in 2019-2020.StatsCan also says international undergraduates pay almost five times more on average in tuition fees than Canadian students. The average tuition fees of undergraduate Canadian students rose by 27.8 per cent in 2010-2011 to $6,580 in 2020-2021, while those for undergraduate international students almost doubled to $32,039."Because tuition fees and enrolments of international students are growing at a much faster pace than their Canadian counterparts, their overall contribution to total tuition revenues at Canadian universities has risen. This has helped to make up for the reduction of provincial funding in universities\' budgets for their operational activities," StatsCan said in a 2024 report. What does the sector need in order to get back to normal?OPSEU says an emergency infusion of $1.4 billion is needed to stabilize the college system. Vollebregt agreed that investment into the sector is necessary. He said across the province, colleges are reducing operations and program offerings to become more sustainable, but he argued it\'s counterintui- tive since post-secondary education is "an incredibly valuable investment for any government, when you consider that highly trained and motivated graduates drive industry and help grow the economy."But now, more than ever, the need to fund colleges has reached an alltime high. That\'s what the sector needs so it can get back on its feet, Vollebregt said."Rather than one specific thing, it\'s really an investment into the college system," he said."We\'re looking for partners to invest into us by the provincial government so that we can deliver on the provincial economic agenda and provide the talent that our economy needs, our local communities need. And we can do that, we\'ve been doing it for 60 years and we\'ll do it for 60 more. We need that trust and investment into our system."Postmedia has reached out to Ontario\'s Ministry of Colleges and Universities for comment.- With files from Postmedia Network and The Canadian Press']
